issue: In a federal criminal prosecution under CIPA, must the government's state-secrets privilege claim over classified information be formally invoked by the head of the department that controls the information, or may a lower-ranked official invoke it?
provision: Classified Information Procedures Act, 18 U.S.C. app. 3 § 4; United States v. Reynolds, 345 U.S. 1 (1953)

sides.position: Formal invocation of the state-secrets privilege requires a declaration by the head of the department with control over the matter (or its political head), as Reynolds requires, even in criminal cases under CIPA.
cases: United States v. Aref, 533 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 2008)
United States v. Alahmedalabdaloklah, 94 F.4th 782 (9th Cir. 2023)

sides.position: The agency head need not personally invoke the privilege in criminal matters under CIPA; a lower-level official's invocation suffices.
cases: United States v. Rosen, 557 F.3d 192 (4th Cir. 2009)
United States v. El-Mezain, 664 F.3d 467 (5th Cir. 2011)

this_court: Requires formal invocation by the department head; the Ninth Circuit adheres to its prior CIPA decisions and to Reynolds, although it excuses the government's noncompliance in this case.
quote: Other circuit courts are divided on this issue.
cite: United States v. Ahmed Alahmedalabdaloklah, 94 F.4th 782 (9th Cir. 2023)
